newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan bankruptcy debt soars 97% in Jan-June period.
newsitem.headline: Japan bankruptcy debt soars 97% in Jan-June period.

text.p: Japan's feeble economic recovery continues to generate a high level of business failures and more Japanese firms are likely to join the nation's lengthening insolvency list, a private research firm said on Monday.

Total debts held by Japanese firms that went bust in the six months to June soared 96.8 percent from the same period a year earlier to 6.33 trillion yen ($55.5 billion), Tokyo Shoko Research Ltd said in a report.
The figure was the highest ever for a January-June period, surpassing the previous record of 3.95 trillion yen ($34.6 billion) marked in the first half of 1995.
The total number of firms that went under during the half-year period climbed 9.1 percent from the same period a year earlier to 7,933 cases, it said.
Japan's economy is gradually picking up, but the gap between large businesses and small and medium-sized businesses is widening, Tokyo Shoko said in the report.

Bankruptcies were more evident among small and medium-sized companies, which are struggling to adjust to structural changes after the bursting of the nation's "bubble" of inflated asset prices in the late 1980s.

The rise in Japan's national sales tax in April had a major negative impact on sales, while business failures in the construction sector remained high due to declines in private capital spending and public works projects, it said.
"Despite strong expectations of economic recovery in the second half of this year, bankruptcies are expected to grow further," Tokyo Shoko Research said in the report.

Japanese firms which still hold massive debts from the bubble era, as well as those which cannot turn a profit in the face of structural problems, will eventually be restructured or disappear, the research firm said.
In June alone, total bankruptcy debt in Japan fell 49.5 percent year-on-year to 384.45 billion yen ($3.37 billion), while the number of bankruptcy cases surged by 18.7 percent to 1,336 cases.
The number of bankruptcy cases in June was the ninth highest on record for the month of June, and the fourth month in a row where there were more than 1,300 cases, it said.

The surge in bankruptcy debt in the first half of 1997 was mainly due to the failures of three nonbank financial units of Nippon Credit Bank Ltd. They went bust in April with debts totalling 2.03 trillion yen ($17.8 billion).
Of the three, Crown Leasing Corp had 1.19 trillion yen ($10.4 billion) in debt, making it the nation's largest bankruptcy ever.
Bankruptcies which were a result of a bankruptcy by another firm increased by 50.8 percent to 801 cases in the first-half period over the year-earlier period, it said.

These chain-reaction bankruptcies jumped as companies whose businesses were hit by the prolonged economic weakness faced difficulties in borrowing money from financial firms, which have become increasingly selective, Tokyo Shoko said.

Business failures in the construction industry, meanwhile, rose by 17.9 percent year-on-year to 2,335 cases in the January-June period, marking the seventh consecutive year of rises in the period, it said.

The number of business failures in the industry remained at a high level in June, when bankruptcy cases rose 30 percent from a year earlier to 420. It was the second time this year that bankruptcies in the sector surpassed 400 cases.
Tokyo Shoko quoted a city bank official as saying in the report that banks may not always be in a situation where they can support troubled companies, as doing so will also put the banks in trouble.

Earlier this month, medium-sized general contractor Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd applied for court protection with 511 billion yen ($4.48 billion) in debt, becoming the first listed general contractor to go under in the nation's post-war history. ($1=114 yen)
